Japan Joint Staff Office map Suspected Russian aircraft violated Japanese territorial airspace twice on Thursdays, prompting fighter aircraft to be scrambled in response, Japan’s Defense Minister announced Tuesday. Between 4:07 and 4:10 a.m. on Thursday, one suspected Russian aircraft violated Japanese airspace northwest of Okinoshima, which lies in the East China Sea, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said in his regularly scheduled Tuesday press conference. Subsequently, between 4:09 and 4:12 a.m., a second suspected Russian aircraft violated Japanese airspace in the same area. The aircraft passed through the Tsushima Strait, flew between Yonaguni Island and Taiwan, and proceeded into the Philippine Sea. Japan Air Self-Defense Force fighter aircraft from the JASDF’s Western Air Defense Command were scrambled in response. The Japanese aircraft issued notifications and warnings to the suspected Russian aircraft. Japan’s aircraft were unable to see the Russian aircraft and visually confirm the type of aircraft that entered the airspace. “Whilst it is difficult to state with certainty the intent or purpose behind the Russian aircraft’s actions on this occasion, the Ministry of Defense and the Self-Defense Forces will, in any case, continue to monitor Russia’s military movements with the utmost attention and will take every possible measure to ensure vigilance, surveillance and appropriate responses to airspace violations,” said Koizumi, according to a transcript of the conference . Koizumi called the violation of Japan’s territorial airspace by Russian aircraft not only a serious infringement of Japan’s sovereignty but also a threat to Japan’s security. The Japanese government has lodged a protest with the Russian government through diplomatic channels and demanded that such incidents not be repeated, Koizumi said. The Russian aircraft entered the Air Defense Identification Zones (ADIZs) of Japan, South Korea and Taiwan on Thursday. An ADIZ begins where sovereign airspace ends and is a defined stretch of international airspace in which aircraft are detected and tracked in the interest of national security. Fighter aircraft are often scrambled to intercept and shadow the foreign aircraft until it leaves the ADIZ. While not recognized under international law, a number of countries have ADIZs because territorial airspace extends just 12 nautical miles from a country’s coastline. The three countries did not identify the Russian aircraft. Two Tu-95MS bombers and two IL-76 transports landed at Da Nang International Airport, Vietnam, later that day, according to local aviation spotters. A Da Nang-based community social media page posted photos of the bombers arriving and videos of the four Russian aircraft parked at the airport. Russia nor Vietnam, as of publication, have issued official statements on the presence of the bombers in Vietnam. A Russian Tu-95 bomber photographed June 27, 2026, by Japanese forces. Japan Joint Staff Office photo In 2015, Reuters reported that the U.S. had requested Vietnam to stop allowing Russian tanker aircraft to use Cam Ranh Bay. The tankers were reportedly being used to refuel Russian bombers that conducted provocative flights near Guam. The last known Russian bomber deployment to Southeast Asia was on Dec. 5, 2017, when two Tu-95MS bombers and two Il-76 transports landed on Biak Island, Indonesia. The Indonesian Air Force said that the visit was for a navigation exercise. The Russian Defense Ministry said at the time that the bombers were refuelled in the air by Ilyushin Il-78 tankers over the Pacific Ocean. The last time a Russian aircraft violated Japanese airspace was on Sept. 23, 2024 , when a Russian IL-38 Maritime Patrol Aircraft violated Japan’s territorial airspace three times north of Rebun Island. The Defense Minister Minoru Kihara said at the time that JASDF F-15J and F-35 Lightning II fighter aircraft were scrambled and discharged flares after the Russian aircraft appeared to have ignored the warnings issued. The incident was the first time Japan had released flares against foreign aircraft.

In a post on Monday, the far-right minister, who previously called for a nuclear bomb to be dropped on Gaza, said he had contacted Interior Minister Gideon Sa’ar, accusing Andrey of "conducting a systematic and wide-ranging delegitimization campaign, based on deliberate deception, distortion of facts, and the dissemination of false and biased reports against the State of Israel and its security forces". This led him to join activist initiatives, initially in Tel Aviv and Jerusalem and later in the West Bank. In May 2024, he moved to the Palestinian community of Ras Ein al-Auja in the Jordan Valley, initially planning to stay for a month. He began posting daily videos documenting settler incursions and attacks, drawing a growing audience and requests from other Palestinian communities to document violence. He has since become a prominent activist and journalist on social media, reaching 807,000 followers on Instagram alone through his documentation of Israel’s occupation and settler attacks on Palestinian communities. Israeli authorities have barred him from the West Bank until 1 January 2027 following his arrest in October. In his letter to Sa’ar, Chikli also cited Andrey’s accusations that Israel was committing ethnic cleansing. pending.title: Finland’s Iceye bids €2 billion for Italian rocket maker Avio
pending.summary: ROME — Finnish operator Iceye has a made €2 billion cash offer ($2.2 billion) for Italian rocket maker Avio which would integrate Europe’s space capabilities as well as putting Iceye in charge of Avio’s expansion into the U.S. missile business. The proposed deal fits with efforts to reduce reliance on external providers and narrow a widening gap with industry leaders in the U.S. and China. “Europe’s need for sovereign space and defense capabilities is growing. Building the industrial capacity to meet that demand takes years, which makes it critical to invest now,” said Iceye on Tuesday. The firm said it would invest €1 billion in Avio in Italy over five years in a bid to expand the customer base of Avio’s Vega rocket. The Finnish government backed the offer, with Finnish Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen stating, “If completed … a global space industry player will be created, through which the self-sufficient security of supply of Finland’s and all of Europe’s defense will rise to a new level.” Avio said on Tuesday it was considering the offer, while the CEO of Italian state controlled defense group Leonardo, which owns an 18% percent stake in Avio, said he was “pleasantly surprised” by the bid and would consider it. Avio’s board held a first meeting on Tuesday and said it had started assessing the bid, which Iceye said offered a 21.3% premium to the Italian group’s closing price on Monday or a 34.8% premium to its three-month volume-weighted average price. Apart from its European space launch activity, Avio is also a market leader in solid rocket motors for missiles. In September it broke ground in Hurt, Virginia, on a new U..S facility to fulfill an ambition to bring much needed extra capacity to U.S. missile production. Avio has already partnered with Raytheon on production of the Mk 104 dual-thrust rocket motor and has teamed with Lockheed Martin to produce motors at Hurt for Lockheed’s Extended Range GMLRS (ER GMLRS) and Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) programs. An Avio spokesman told Defense News that U.S. government approval would be required in the event of a takeover by Iceye, as well as Italian government approval. In September, Avio announced a nine month order intake of €237 million, of which half was defense related, with the remainder mainly related to its Vega C and Vega E launchers. Iceye said its €41-per-share offer will be launched through wholly owned Italian subsidiary Iris 2 with the aim of delisting the company. Avio shares climbed more than 15% to around €39.5 on the news. Iceye has supplied Ukraine with satellite radar imagery since 2022, and last month signed a letter of intent with Nokia and Ukraine’s Defence Ministry to explore cooperation in space, including sovereign satellite communications. Speaking at an event in Helsinki, Iceye CEO Rafal Modrzewski said the company had held consultations with the parties involved, including governments, before launching the bid, and that it would take a few more months to close the transaction. “It’s a phenomenal combination of capabilities … bringing a full vertical integration, following quite clear industry trends,” Modrzewski said, adding that it would be beneficial for both companies. With material from Reuters by Giulia Segreti and Essi Lehto.

pending.title: Fury in Iran as NYT tries to build case for destroying dams
pending.summary: Officials in Tehran have condemned an unsubstantiated a New York Times report that attempted to link Iran's network of civilian dams to its missile programme , a claim that could be used to justify attacks on the country's water infrastructure should the war resume. In an article published Monday, the New York Times quoted military analysts and water specialists speculating about whether Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps uses dams to provide power to underground missile sites. NYT was unable to find evidence that the infrastructure is used for military purposes, as one of the report's authors admitted. "No conclusive evidence—but questions worth asking," Sanam Mahoozi wrote on X . All seven people interviewed by the newspaper said only it was logical that Iran may have placed military sites close to dams. Deliberately targeting civilians or civilian infrastructure—such as schools, hospitals, water systems, and/or power plants—is strictly prohibited under international law, and constitutes a war crime. Water security expert Nima Shokri said he suspected a link because of a pattern of US airstrikes earlier on in the war , many of which he said occurred near dams. Meanwhile, Israeli defence analyst and Iran specialist Danny Citrinowicz said only that it was reasonable that it could have turned to "autonomous or redundant infrastructure" for its missile bases. Many of the country's dams provide vital water, irrigation and electricity services, making their destruction potentially devastating for millions of Iranians. The NYT report triggered fury in Tehran, where officials threatened to retaliate in kind should the US or Israel strike any of the country's dams. "New rule: Any dam, port, or power plant near a US or Israeli base is dual-use. We'll apply your logic consistently and even-handedly," Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf wrote in a post on X. Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei called the report "baseless" and described it as "yet another example of a malicious campaign to manufacture propaganda and security pretexts aimed at justifying attacks on a country’s vital infrastructure". US intel alleges Iran 'dirty bomb' plot According to another report, this time by CNN , US intelligence officials have claimed that Iran is planning to target Trump administration officials with a 'dirty bomb' or chemical weapon in Washington. Sources told CNN they had obtained intelligence that included plans to attack specific targets and locations in the US capital, though there is no evidence that Tehran has decided to move forward. But these claims appeared to be contradicted by the White House, which said in a statement that "there are no credible threats to the homeland". There are also disagreements among intelligence officials about the credibility of the intelligence. Iranian officials and military figures have vowed to kill Trump following the US-Israeli assassination of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei on the opening day of the war in February . Posters threatening his life have been seen in Tehran in recent weeks, while demands for his killing have become commonplace among pro-government protesters. At the same time, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent—who has led the administration's renewed assault on Iran's economy—has reportedly been relocated to a military base following threats to his life. Nevertheless, officials disagree about whether Iran would attempt such an attack or has the capabilities to pull it off. "Whether they actually have the personnel in place to execute is a matter of debate," one of CNN's sources said. The reports by these US media outlets come as hawkish voices in DC and Israeli officials push to relaunch an unpopular war amid stalled diplomatic efforts.

In January and February, US Central Command (CENTCOM) transferred 5,704 suspected IS members from Syria to Iraq after the US-backed Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) withdrew from detention facilities where they had been held. Most of the detainees are Iraqi and Syrian nationals. 'Good cooperation' While there are no official figures on the nationalities of those held in Iraq, unofficial reports estimate that around 900 are foreign nationals, including 160 Turks, 10 Dutch citizens, nine Britons, four Swedes, three French nationals, 13 Australians and 130 Russians. The sources, who requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue, said Iraqi authorities had reaffirmed their commitment to working with the international community to resolve the detainee file. They described cooperation as progressing well, saying Baghdad had told European governments it had addressed shortcomings inherited from the international coalition and the SDF in handling the prisoners. Iraq's Justice Ministry is handling detainee cases under the supervision of the Supreme Judicial Council, with support from security agencies and the army, while prosecutions are being carried out according to Iraq's counterterrorism law. Ex-Prime Minister Mohammed Shia al-Sudani said in February that the transfer of IS prisoners from Syria had been an Iraqi decision aimed at protecting national, regional and international security. He urged other countries to cooperate and repatriate their detained nationals. European concerns over lenient sentences Under the agreement, detainees will be investigated and tried in Iraq according to international standards, with a guarantee that they will not be handed death sentences. Iraq has also agreed to return prisoners to countries seeking their repatriation once their trials are completed and verdicts issued. The sources said European governments wanted trials to take place in Iraq because they feared their own courts would impose what they consider lenient sentences for terrorism offences. Convicted detainees could then be transferred to their home countries if requested. Last month, Human Rights Watch (HRW) warned that detainees faced the risk of unfair trials and the death penalty as countries delayed repatriating their nationals. The organisation said dozens of governments had failed to bring home citizens detained in Iraq or provide them with adequate assistance, amid allegations of torture, medical neglect and deaths in custody. HRW cited claims by five foreign detainees that they had been tortured during interrogations after their transfer to Iraq. Lawyers also reported abuses intended to extract false confessions. Iraqi authorities, particularly the judiciary, have sought to reassure European governments about the fairness of trials and the treatment of prisoners. As evidence of judicial impartiality, Iraqi officials pointed to the acquittal of hundreds of Syrians charged with terrorism offences. An Iraqi court recently ordered the release of around 500 Syrian detainees, whom Baghdad is preparing to return to Syria in batches, the sources said. Iraq seeks support for prison construction Iraq has also called on European countries to honour their commitments to help manage the detainee crisis, particularly by providing financial assistance to build prisons capable of accommodating those held. HRW quoted Ali Diaa, deputy head of Iraq's National Centre for International Judicial Cooperation, which is overseeing the investigations into the detainees, who urged the international community to take responsibility for its citizens. "We are looking for tangible support, not workshops and conferences," he said. The sources also described cooperation between Iraqi judicial authorities and US and British intelligence agencies in tracking IS remnants and other militant groups as "good". They said British officials consistently insist on legal cover for all joint operations and cooperation, a position Iraqi authorities understand and appreciate. Previous reports have warned that IS could launch attacks to free its members held in Iraq. However, Iraqi security assessments shared with European governments indicate that the group retains only small sleeper cells and clandestine networks in desert areas. The sources said these groups were now too weak to seize cities or carry out the large-scale operations IS once conducted.

Serbian arms exports to Israel rose from $1.5m to $45.8m in 2024, according to a joint investigation by the Balkan Investigative Reporting Network and Haaretz. The surge coincided with Israel’s genocide in Gaza. Serbia also stepped up its purchases of Israeli weapons. In early 2025, it bought Elbit Systems’ PULS artillery systems and Hermes drones for $335m. In August that year, it bought long-range missiles, drones and electronic warfare equipment for about $1.6bn. Elbit, the controversial Israeli arms manufacturer, has sought to expand in the Balkans in recent years, pursuing factory projects in Serbia and Albania. 'The issue is how to implement this break gradually without fully destroying the partnership with Israel, and without making Israel an enemy' - Vuk Vuksanovic, King’s College How Elbit’s investments in Serbia and the country’s ties with Israel will develop “remains uncertain”, Vuk Vuksanovic, a lecturer in foreign policy and grand strategy at King’s College London’s Department of War Studies, told Middle East Eye. “Serbian society has been historically divided on the Israeli-Palestinian issue, with some Serbs having emotional ties with the global Jewish community over the shared victimhood from World War II,” said Vuksanovic. “At the same time, many Serbs have expressed solidarity with Palestinians given the legacy of non-aligned Yugoslavia. “In the past couple of years, especially with the rise of the Student Movement, we see increasing solidarity with Palestinians,” said Vuksanovic. Vuksanovic warned that “while the desire and intention are noble and sincere, in practice this will be tougher to implement, as it has yet to be seen how to deprive the military industry of income, how to break technological and supply chain links set with the Elbit factory, and how firm the legal obligations stipulated in the contracts are. “The issue is how to implement this break gradually without fully destroying the partnership with Israel, and without making Israel an enemy, and potentially its interest groups in the US,” he added. “Paradoxically, this relationship may prove harder to transform than Serbia’s relations with the EU, the US, Russia, and China.” MEE contacted the Student List for comment and had received no response by the time of publication. A spokesperson for the Charity Commission also confirmed to The New Arab that it has "opened a regulatory compliance case into JW3 Trust Limited to assess concerns raised." It added: "We will be engaging with the charity’s trustees to gather more information and determine if there is any regulatory role for the Commission." Shaima Dallali, a researcher at the ICJP said that the real test would be whether the Charity Commission now launches a credible investigation into the UK-registered charity, which is based in Camden, London. “The Charity Commission opening a case into JW3 is a welcome step, but opening a case is not accountability,” Dallali told The New Arab . “For years, we have presented the regulator with evidence of UK charities directly funding illegal Israeli settlements, yet meaningful action has been sorely lacking.” She continued: “Now we have a UK charity whose premises were used to promote jobs in those same settlements. This raises serious questions about the charity’s involvement, its trustees’ responsibilities and potential criminal liability.” According to the ICJP, the MedEx UK event, held at JW3 in Camden on 25 October, was primarily organised by the Israeli government and aimed to recruit UK-based medical professionals to work in Israel. However, promotional materials distributed at the event advertised vacancies at medical facilities in Israeli settlements in the West Bank and the occupied Syrian Golan Heights . Leaflets distributed by Israeli healthcare provider Terem reportedly advertised positions at clinics in the occupied West Bank settlements of Ma’ale Adumim, Beitar Illit and Modi’in Illit, as well as Katzrin in the Golan Heights. Israeli settlements in both territories are illegal under international law, and the UK government recently announced sanctions against firms operating there. “The Commission has the evidence before it. What we need now is action, not another case that quietly disappears into the regulator’s files,” Dallali told The New Arab. “The real test is not whether the Commission investigates, but whether it is prepared to hold charities to account.” The Charity Commission's latest action follows an earlier investigation by UK broadcaster Sky News , which also highlighted the event's efforts to recruit Jewish doctors in London to work in Israeli settlements. The event was advertised as a “can’t miss event for doctors and medical students from across the United Kingdom who are considering Aliyah”, according to Sky News . The term "Aliyah" refers to Jewish people emigrating to Israel. The event also reportedly offered attendees the opportunity to network with healthcare recruiters and begin the Israeli Ministry of Health's licensing process. Following the reports, pro-Palestine campaigners condemned the event, as the UK government prepared further sanctions over Israeli settlement activity. In a statement, Andy McDonald MP, Labour co-chair of the Britain-Palestine All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG), said: “UK sanctions are currently making their way through parliament.” He added: “When concluded, they will be capable of immediately closing down such events with full legal consequences for the organisers.” The developments come after UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced a new sanctions package , the first since the government's September reset of its approach to Israeli actions in the West Bank, amid a surge in settler attacks on Palestinians and their property. The government said sanctions against eight construction and property development companies would disrupt their financial flows and ability to support settlement construction in the West Bank. The measures also target Tzav 9 , an Israeli extremist group which has carried out blockades to prevent humanitarian aid from entering Gaza.

pending.title: Syria sentences officer to life for killing five in Suweida
pending.summary: A military criminal court in Damascus sentenced a member of Syria's Internal Security Forces to life imprisonment on Tuesday after convicting him of killing five civilians in the southern province of Suweida in February this year. Ezz al-Din Ibrahim bin Abdul Aziz, was found guilty of deliberately murdering five Suweida residents. He was also given an additional 10-year prison sentence for attempting to kill a sixth person, who survived with injuries. The case dates back to 7 February 2026, when the defendant fired on a group of civilians working in an olive grove in al-Matouna village in northern Suweida province, despite their having obtained prior security clearance to access and work on their land. Four people were killed at the scene, while a fifth later died from his injuries. A sixth person was wounded but survived. The incident highlighted the dangers facing civilians in areas affected by the volatile security situation in Suweida, particularly when attempting to access their agricultural land and carry out their daily work. The verdict is significant because the defendant was a member of Syria's security forces, and because it comes within the framework of the judicial process addressing cases linked to violence in Suweida. In July 2025, sectarian violence broke out in Suweida between Druze, who form a majority of the province's population and mostly Sunni Bedouin tribes, killing hundreds of people. Government forces intervened but were accused of war crimes and sectarian attacks themselves. Israel also intervened, carrying out airstrikes targeting sites in Suweida and Damascus. The province is now largely controlled by pro-Israeli Druze militias opposed to the Syrian government. The violence left over 1,700 dead, thousands of people wounded and tens of thousands displaced. The verdict is one of the first rulings issued by the military criminal court tasked with handling these cases and has brought attention to efforts to ensure accountability for government personnel accused of violations against civilians. Following the killings in February, Syrian authorities announced the arrest of an Internal Security Forces member. At the time, the government's Internal Security chief for Suweida, Hossam Maamoun al-Tahan, said abuses against civilians were unacceptable and that the authorities wouldn't tolerate actions threatening residents' safety. The ruling comes at a time when accountability for violations in Suweida remains a major challenge for the Syrian government, with growing calls to prosecute anyone implicated in the killings and attacks against civilians. In March, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Syria stressed the need to expand accountability measures and investigate the responsibility of individuals from all sides involved in the Suweida violence, describing this as essential to achieving justice and rebuilding trust between local communities. Syria's national investigative committee into the events in Suweida also announced that it had uncovered evidence implicating members of government security and military forces, as well as members of irregular armed groups and other parties, in violations. Information concerning suspected perpetrators was subsequently referred to judicial authorities.

An October report by SIPRI found that development assistance cuts in Britain and Germany make only a limited contribution to financing their military build-ups, while potentially carrying significant humanitarian consequences. For countries already affected by conflict, displacement and economic crises, the consequences could extend to food assistance, healthcare and education, Xiao Liang, a researcher at SIPRI's Military Expenditure and Arms Production Programme and one of the authors of the report, told The New Arab . "In the Middle East, countries like Syria, Yemen, Lebanon and Palestine are particularly vulnerable as they are heavily dependent on [Official Development Assistance] ODA funding, so aid cuts can directly affect access to basic needs such as food assistance, healthcare and education, especially for displaced people and vulnerable communities," he said. SIPRI's analysis examines falling assistance alongside rising military expenditure, focusing on Britain and Germany as examples of the competing budget priorities. "In the case of [the] UK, Syria, Yemen and West Bank/Gaza are among its top ODA recipients so they will be most exposed to the cuts," Liang said. Limited savings, immediate consequences Liang's warning highlights the regional stakes of decisions being made in European capitals, with Britain providing one of the clearest examples of an explicit trade-off between aid and military spending. The government announced in 2025 that it would reduce its aid target from 0.5 percent of gross national income to 0.3 percent by 2027 to help finance higher military expenditure. The report compared a projected $600 million reduction in British ODA between 2025 and 2026 with a planned $5.6 billion increase in military spending in 2026. The aid reduction amounts to around 11 percent of the military increase. "A key point in this comparison is that ODA levels are very small compared to military spending to begin with, which means even cutting ODA to zero will not compensate for the long-term military build-up plans for countries like [the] UK," Liang told TNA . Germany presents a similar imbalance. Its military spending is expected to roughly double by 2030 from its 2025 level of $114 billion, while ODA is expected to decline from 0.56 percent of national income in 2025 to approximately 0.43 percent by 2029. The planned military spending increase is more than ten times larger than the planned aid reduction, SIPRI found. "Cuts to development aid make only a marginal contribution to the financing of Germany’s military expansion while substantially reducing resources available for international development," the report stated. The timing of the consequences also differs. Major military procurement programmes can take years to produce operational capabilities, while aid reductions can affect humanitarian and development programmes much sooner. "Military spending, particularly major procurement programmes, can take years to translate into actual capabilities. In contrast, reductions in ODA can affect development and humanitarian programmes much more immediately," the researchers wrote. For the Middle East, Liang also pointed to the importance of assistance delivered through international organisations, rather than solely through direct relationships between donor and recipient governments. The big picture: Unlike a nuclear weapon, a "dirty bomb" uses common explosives to scatter radioactive material, potentially contaminating surrounding areas, forcing evacuations and causing widespread disruption. Driving the news: Asked Tuesday about reports of a possible Iranian dirty bomb plot in Washington, Trump said, "We're looking into it." "We take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," he added . Trump did not say an attack was imminent: "I hope it's not." Trump warned Iran would face unprecedented consequences if it carried out an attack. Catch up quick: Trump's comments came hours after CNN reported about the threat to D.C. CNN reported that unnamed officials described Iran's attack planning as "an effort to give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack." "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland," says Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman. Iran has denied the allegations, with Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei calling them "baseless." Read more about dirty bombs below. What is a dirty bomb? How it works: A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives, like dynamite, with radioactive materials, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . This is much different than a nuclear bomb. A nuclear bomb splits atoms and releases a huge blast of energy. Dirty bombs spread radioactive dust, smoke or other material that contaminate, the CDC says. How dangerous is a dirty bomb? The main danger stems from the explosion itself, which, like other explosive materials, can cause serious injuries and damage, according to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission . The scope of impact would depend on the size of the bomb, NRC says, as well as the type of radioactive material and weather conditions — especially if the material is inhaled. "Because people cannot see, smell, feel, or taste radiation, you should take immediate steps to protect yourself and your loved ones," the CDC says. The biggest concerns from high levels of radiation exposure would be nausea, vomiting, skin burns and radiation sickness, per CDC. Yes, but: The exposure would probably not cause immediate serious illness, the CDC says, except for those very close to the blast. What would happen if one exploded in Washington? Though the White House confirms there are no credible threats, there are plans in place to keep D.C. safe from threats. The Department of Homeland Security 's immediate response includes police and responders restricting access to affected areas, while experts investigate radiation levels. Residents may be told to shelter indoors. DHS' Securing the Cities program helps high-risk metro areas, including D.C. and its region, detect and prevent potential attacks. The DHS has provided $300 million to the STC areas through 2023 to help them buy radiation detectors, train officers and build systems for spotting potential radioactive materials. Worthy of your time: The NRC recommends staying as far away as possible from the bomb site. The CDC has tips on what to do if you're in a home, building or car when a dirty bomb goes off. Removing outer clothing may eliminate up to 90% of radioactive dust, the CDC says. Pets should also be brought inside, the CDC says. Has a dirty bomb ever been used? No dirty bomb has ever been successfully used in an attack, according to the Washington Post and other reports , though authorities have uncovered several plots and attempts. The U.S. Government Accountability Office has tracked past attempts, including multiple attempts in Russia. In 2002, U.S. authorities arrested Jose Padilla, an American accused of discussing a dirty-bomb attack with al-Qaeda operatives, potentially targeting Washington, D.C., per the Department of Justice . The alleged plot was in its early stages and never materialized. The bottom line: A dirty bomb attack doesn't appear to be imminent in the U.S., but any such strike would make a relatively small explosion into a much larger public safety crisis.

pending.title: US scolds Ukraine over deep strikes ahead of fresh Russia peace talks
pending.summary: BRUSSELS — U.S. deputy Pentagon chief Elbridge Colby on Tuesday hit out at Ukraine for its long-range strike campaign against Russia — a fresh blow to Kyiv as it seeks to shore up its negotiating position during peace talks with Moscow. His comments, made at a meeting primarily aimed at raising further support for Ukraine, come as the U.S. is expected to hold fresh peace negotiations with Ukraine and Russia in the coming weeks. “While the public conversation focuses on the spectacle of deep strikes designed to incur pain on the Russian population, our assessment is that such strikes have not been effective … nor do they contribute to blunting Russia’s advances on the front line,” Colby said at a meeting of the Ukrainian Defense Contact Group defense ministers in Brussels. “Such strikes, especially those that target civilian infrastructure … have actually probably hardened the Russian public’s resolve and the Kremlin’s own willingness to escalate,” he said, adding: “The balance of advantage in deep strikes may well favor Moscow.” The comments prompted an immediate rebuke from Ukraine’s NATO allies. “Criticizing strikes like that in Russia to destroy strategic military … targets is quite a stupid thing,” German Foreign Minister Boris Pistorius said after the meeting. “Instead of criticizing that, we should rather criticize and talk about [Russia’s] terroristic strikes every night.” “It’s not for us to tell Ukraine how to fight their war,” U.K. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters. “In terms of deep strike capability, there’s no doubt in my mind that it’s helped to degrade [Russian President Vladimir] Putin’s war machine.” Ukraine has in recent months stepped up long-range attacks deep inside Russia, targeting depots of the online retailer Wildberries, military facilities, oil refineries and fuel export facilities. It says it has taken out 30% of Russian oil refining capacity. On Tuesday, Ukraine said it had destroyed part of the Kerch bridge linking Russia to Crimea. Washington has long opposed deep strikes against Russia, particularly those that affect oil infrastructure. U.S. President Donald Trump last month accused Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war. Zelenskyy has previously said the strikes give Ukraine “equal footing” in negotiations with Russia. Moscow has also pummeled Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Funding for Ukraine Colby urged ministers to keep funding the NATO-backed PURL program, where Ukrainian allies pay for American weapons for Kyiv. “Sustaining the flow of critical munitions is essential for Ukrainian troops to continue holding the front line,” he said. PURL was set up last year after the U.S. stopped directly funding Ukraine’s war effort following Trump’s return to power. On Tuesday, several countries including Germany, Norway and Sweden announced over $300 million in fresh contributions to the scheme. The U.K. separately announced £240 million in air defense support, including over 1,000 short-range missiles and a dozen air defense radars. NATO allies are still billions short of meeting a €70 billion alliance military aid target for Ukraine this year, and a separate goal of raising at least €12 billion for PURL. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte told POLITICO he was “cautiously optimistic” allies could still meet the overall target, set at the alliance’s July summit in Ankara. Despite the criticism of long-range strikes, Colby praised Ukraine’s “very effective” use of mid-range strike drones to “deny Russian advances” on the front line. Ukraine last week said it had detected limitations on critical U.S. Starlink satellite services for the second time in two months, a move Kyiv said made it more difficult to intercept Russian drones. Asked about the latest restrictions, Colby demurred, telling reporters: “We are very focused on supporting Ukraine’s ability to defend itself and these … mid-range strikes, and we’re taking steps that are consistent with that policy.”

previous_post.fa_title: بسته شدن کامل آسمان مولداوی در پی پرواز پهپاد ساخت ایران
paras: مقامات مولداوی پس از رویت و ضبط تصاویر یک فروند پهپاد انتحاری گران-۲ (نسخه روسی پهپاد شاهد-۱۳۶) در آسمان پایتخت، تمام حریم هوایی این کشور را به دلایل امنیتی مسدود کردند. طبق اعلام وزارت دفاع مولداوی، مرکز عملیات هوایی ارتش ورود چندین پهپاد را به حریم هوایی این کشور ردگیری کرده است.

بر اساس گزارش‌های نظامی، این پهپاد دلتا بال دو بار متوالی ظرف کمتر از نیم ساعت از سمت مرزهای اوکراین وارد حریم هوایی مولداوی شد. پس از رویت پهپاد در بخش‌های شمالی کیشیناو و شنیده شدن صدای موتور آن توسط شهروندان، دستور ممنوعیت فوری پروازها صادر شد.

نیروهای نظامی مولداوی اعلام کردند که پایش حریم هوایی ادامه دارد و هشدار امینتی ویژه‌ای به شهروندان برای عدم نزدیک شدن به بقایای احتمالی پهپادها داده شده است. این حادثه تازه ترین مورد از نقض حریم هوایی مولداوی در جریان درگیری‌های منطقه‌ای به شمار می‌رود.

ready.fa_title: هشدار رئیس‌جمهور مولداوی درباره نقض حریم هوایی با پهپادهای شاهد
paras: مایا ساندو، رئیس‌جمهور مولداوی، پس از بستن حریم هوایی این کشور اعلام کرد چند فروند پهپاد روسی حریم هوایی مولداوی را نقض کرده‌اند که دست‌کم یکی از آن‌ها بر فراز پایتخت دیده شده است. او تأکید کرد که جنگ روسیه کل اروپا را تهدید می‌کند و کیشیناو به همراهی با اوکراین و تلاش برای تحریم مسکو ادامه خواهد داد.

وزارت دفاع مولداوی اعلام کرد حریم هوایی کشور ساعت ۱۶:۲۷ به وقت محلی پس از رصد حرکت پهپادی از نوع شاهد از سمت جنوب به سوی منطقه بوتانیکا در کیشیناو مسدود شد. هم‌زمان، وزیر امور خارجه مولداوی این رویداد را نقض جدی حاکمیت ملی و تهدیدی مستقیم برای ایمنی شهروندان خواند و خواستار توقف این اقدامات شد.

پلیس مولداوی اعلام کرد تماس‌های متعددی از سوی ساکنان پایتخت و منطقه فلورشتی مبنی بر شنیده شدن صدای انفجار و غرش‌های مهیب دریافت کرده است. وزارت دفاع نیز از شهروندان خواست از لمس هرگونه شیء پرنده مشکوک به دلیل احتمال وجود مواد منفجره خودداری کنند.

paras: سخنگوی وزارت خارجه ایران گزارش شبکه سی‌ان‌ان مبنی بر برنامه‌ریزی تهران برای انجام حمله با بمب کثیف در واشنگتن را به‌شدت رد کرد و این اتهامات را بی‌اساس خواند.
پیش‌تر این شبکه خبری به نقل از منابع اطلاعاتی مدعی شده بود که ایران در حال تدوین طرح‌هایی برای این حمله احتمالی در پایتخت ایالات متحده است.
به دنبال انتشار این گزارش، دونالد ترامپ، رئیس‌جمهور آمریکا، با هشدار به ایران مدعی شد که آن‌ها بهای سنگینی خواهند پرداخت که تاکنون هیچ کشوری پرداخت نکرده است.

posted_events.fa_title: ادعای زلنسکی درباره دریافت ماهانه ده‌ها موشک توسط روسیه از کره شمالی
